chapter: French Opera house and cello teachers
title: Studying cello with the opera cellist and then Mr. Tio
summary: He tells how he met a French opera cellist through a bar and ballroom run by his widow, took cello and harmony lessons from him, and later studied with Mr. Tio.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: I went away to Europe, and he'd pick up a troupe here. And there were certain musicians that lived here, that came here formerly with an opera company, that stayed here, and they were always signed up. Right. They were always signed up for when the orchestra would come and play. And this man, initially, Scott was his name. He was born in Toulouse, France, and he got his first education there. And he had his musical education in France, in Paris Conservatory. And he studied in Myron, Michigan. And he was, I believe, the chief cellist in that office with a kid. Because they always had, they always used three or four cellists, you know. Oh, yeah. And I got acquainted with him for Mr. Beaufort. Now Beaufort is a man that taught my friend trombone, Benny Raytheon. And when Benny used to go for his lesson, I used to go with him, you see. And we got well acquainted with him and so forth. And after he died, he had a little wine place on Charles Street. Not very far from where he lived. Between, I think it was between Toulouse and Madison. You know that little place there. And after he died, well, his wife kept it in place. So in later years, she opened the ballroom on Charles, between St. Louis and Toulouse, on the Riverside. And I was coming from the post office with me and my friend, Mr. Charlemagne, and all musicians, Mr. McNeil. And we was coming along and she was standing outside and she recognized me. Oh, she said, the friends of my old husband, she said, come right on in. So she took us back in that dining room because at that time, the law had changed. We either had a barroom for white or for colored. Well, in that neighborhood, she couldn't think of having a barroom for colored. There was no colored people around there. And so she has to say, well, you come right in and come back in my dining room. So we used to go back in the dining room. And in the afternoon when we used to leave, we used to pass there. We'd go back there and have drinks and everything else. We used to like to drink. You know how young fellas are. And so forth. And the opera, when the opera was there, all the musicians used to go there. She being a Frenchman herself, you understand? And she had an adopted son. She had no children. Oh, she had an adopted son. His name was Paul, like me. And Paul used to come back there. And they used to come back there and we all used to drink and go on. And that's why I met Mr. Lescar. He was interested in me because, of course, you know those fellas, they won't take any people unless you have some kind of a background. Well, he gave me a quiz and everything else and so forth and so forth. And he says, you've been well instructed. I said, well, it's nothing like being well instructed anyway. So he was stopping at Miss Vignard on St. Louis near Boyville. And I went there for lessons. I took lessons with him there. He taught me the cello. I had already taken some lessons with Professor Dickerson. But he taught me all over again. And I took lessons with him. And he began to give me, he was a harmonist too. He began to teach me a harmony when he had to leave. You see, he left. So that's why I went to Mr. T. O. And Mr. T. O. taught me all over again. And of which, you know you never get through.
